notes: - Marine biologist Nadia Oyelaran surveyed marine growth on 40 concrete pilings at the Cutler Bay municipal pier.
- Divers scraped and weighed samples from four depth zones on each piling, from the waterline down to 4 meters.
- Barnacles made up the largest share of the growth by weight in every zone.
- Mean growth thickness across all pilings was 14 millimeters.
- The pilings were last cleaned 18 months before the survey.
worlds.summary: The survey's central result is clear: barnacles dominated the growth by weight in every zone, and the fouling layer averaged 14 millimeters thick.
worlds.explanationIfShown: These notes state that barnacles made up the largest share of the growth by weight in every zone and that mean thickness was 14 millimeters, so this summary puts the survey's main finding front and center without adding anything the notes do not support. Each other summary names a group the notes never credit with the largest share — blue mussels, tube worms, or sea squirts — and each reports a mean thickness of 19, 24, or 29 millimeters where these notes record 14.

goal: present a cautious summary of the findings

notes: - Occupational health researcher Tomás Herrera measured airborne flour dust in 6 commercial bakeries.
- Each bakery was sampled for one week before and one week after overhead exhaust hoods were installed.
- Average dust concentration fell by 22 percent after installation.
- Levels still exceeded the recommended exposure limit during flour sack emptying.
- The bakeries kept their existing mixing equipment and staffing throughout the study.
worlds.summary: Herrera's findings suggest the hoods helped but did not solve the problem: across the 6 bakeries sampled, average dust fell by roughly 22 percent, yet levels during flour sack emptying still exceeded the recommended limit.
worlds.explanationIfShown: This summary reports exactly what these notes support — 6 bakeries, a 22 percent average drop, and a remaining exceedance during flour sack emptying — and hedges it as a suggestion rather than a settled conclusion, which is what a cautious summary requires. Each other summary claims a sample of 9, 12, or 15 bakeries where these notes say 6, a decline of 38, 51, or 64 percent where these notes say 22, and an exceedance during hand bench dusting, dough sheeting runs, or end-of-day sweeping rather than flour sack emptying.

goal: compare the results of the two conditions

notes: - Transit engineer Marta Ollila ran a six-month trial on the city tram network, applying a rail-head lubricant at 18 curves and leaving 18 matched curves untreated.
- Trackside microphones logged peak wheel squeal at every curve in the study; before treatment, both groups averaged 92 decibels.
- Across the trial, peak squeal at the lubricated curves fell by an average of 7 decibels, while the untreated curves stayed within 1 decibel of their starting level.
- Profile gauges showed flange wear building up at the untreated curves at 2.2 times the rate recorded at the lubricated curves.
- Ollila reports that tram type, service frequency, and ambient temperature were comparable across the two groups.
worlds.summary: Ollila's lubricated curves ran 7 decibels quieter than the untreated curves, which also wore their rail flanges 2.2 times as fast.
worlds.explanationIfShown: These notes record a 7-decibel drop in peak squeal at the lubricated curves and flange wear at the untreated curves accumulating at 2.2 times the lubricated rate, so this sentence sets the two conditions side by side using both measured results. The other summaries report drops of 9, 11, and 13 decibels and wear ratios of 1.1, 2.9, and 1.6 times, each of which contradicts the 7 decibels and 2.2 times these notes actually record.

goal: explain why the finding surprised researchers

notes: - Over one academic year, campus historian Iris Vandermeer catalogued all 8,412 coins recovered from the quad's ornamental fountain during monthly cleanings.
- In a survey run the same year, 600 students almost uniformly reported tossing 'a quarter, for luck,' and quarters were the coin most students carried for the laundry machines.
- Quarters made up just 12 percent of the catalogued coins; pennies and dimes accounted for most of the rest.
- The survey's picture held in only one stretch of the year, during graduation week, when quarters briefly led every other denomination.
- Measured against what the self-reports predicted, the fountain gave up barely half as many coins as expected.
worlds.summary: The census surprised Vandermeer's team because quarters, the coin students almost unanimously reported tossing, made up just 12 percent of the haul, took the lead only during graduation week, and came out of a fountain that yielded barely half as many coins as the survey predicted.
worlds.explanationIfShown: These notes set the students' near-unanimous 'a quarter, for luck' against a catalogue in which quarters were 12 percent of the coins, led only during graduation week, and came from a fountain yielding barely half as many coins as predicted, which is exactly the gap between expectation and result that makes the finding surprising. The other summaries put the quarter share at 19, 26, or 33 percent, place the exception after home football weekends, during first-year move-in week, or in December cleanings, and describe hauls of about two-thirds as many, roughly as many, or nearly twice as many coins, none of which these notes report.

goal: acknowledge a limitation of the study

notes: - Dr. Priya Anand tested whether shade cloth reduces heat stress in greenhouse lettuce.
- She grew lettuce under four shade-cloth densities—30, 40, 50, and 60 percent—and weighed the harvested leaves.
- Yield increased with shade density up to 50 percent and fell at 60 percent.
- Every plot was planted with a single cultivar, 'Salinas'.
- Daytime air temperature was held at one fixed level for the entire trial.
worlds.summary: Anand's result is limited in scope, however: because every plot grew the single cultivar 'Salinas' and daytime air temperature was held at one fixed level, the 50 percent optimum may not hold for other cultivars or at other temperatures.
worlds.explanationIfShown: The notes state that every plot was planted with 'Salinas' and that daytime air temperature was held at one fixed level, so this sentence names exactly the two conditions the trial never varied. The other summaries name a cultivar the notes do not use—'Nevada', 'Concept', or 'Parris Island'—and claim the fixed variable was relative humidity, irrigation volume, or carbon dioxide concentration, none of which the notes mention.

goal: emphasize the practical application of the research

notes: - Marine engineer Tomás Vidal tested a solar-powered LED beacon built for harbor navigation buoys.
- Conventional buoy beacons run on sealed batteries that crews must replace from a boat every six months.
- A fully charged solar beacon kept flashing for twelve days with no sunlight at all.
- The beacons stayed lit through dense fog during the winter test.
- Vidal calculates that crews would service each solar beacon once every five years.
worlds.summary: Vidal's beacon is ready for working harbors: because a charged unit stays lit for twelve days without sun and kept flashing through dense fog, crews could service each buoy once every five years instead of every six months.
worlds.explanationIfShown: The notes give twelve days of operation without sunlight, dense fog as the winter condition the beacons survived, and a five-year service interval against the current six months, so this sentence turns those figures into the maintenance saving harbors would actually see. The other summaries claim eighteen, nine, or fifteen days without sun, storm-driven waves, heavy snowfall, or sub-freezing temperatures as the test condition, and three-, four-, or two-year service intervals—none of which the notes report.

notes: - Conservator Naomi Okafor tracked 60 outdoor community murals in one city for five years.
- Each mural was photographed annually under standardized lighting, and color intensity was measured from the images.
- Across the whole sample, the murals lost an average of 27 percent of their original color intensity over the five years.
- Fading was fastest on murals painted on stucco, which lost color more quickly than murals on any other surface.
- Okafor found no difference in fading between murals made by professional artists and those made by volunteer crews.
worlds.summary: Okafor's five-year survey found that the murals lost an average of 27 percent of their color intensity, with the fastest fading on murals painted on stucco.
worlds.explanationIfShown: The notes give the sample-wide loss as 27 percent and name stucco as the surface that lost color fastest, so this summary states the study's headline result exactly as measured. Each competing summary breaks against these notes on both slots: the notes say 27 percent, not 12, 34, or 19 percent, and they say stucco faded fastest, not metal panels, concrete, or brick.

goal: present a cautious summary of the findings

notes: - Agronomist Priya Raghavan compared 24 apple orchard blocks, half sheltered by hedgerow windbreaks and half unsheltered, across three growing seasons.
- Blocks were matched for variety, soil type, and irrigation, and the fruit from each block was weighed at harvest every season.
- Sheltered blocks yielded on average 11 percent more fruit per tree than unsheltered blocks.
- Fruit from sheltered blocks averaged about 5 grams heavier than fruit from unsheltered blocks.
- The yield difference was concentrated in blocks of trees aged 6 to 10 years, with other blocks showing little difference.

goal: compare the results of the two conditions

notes: - Ines Vargas, a conservation librarian, tested whether a UV-blocking window film slows the fading of paper stored on open shelves.
- She mounted identical dyed-paper test strips behind two banks of south-facing windows: one bank was covered with the film, the other was left untreated.
- Both banks received the same daily sun exposure over a nine-month trial.
- Strips behind the filmed windows lost 12 percent of their original color intensity.
- Strips behind the untreated windows lost 45 percent of their original color intensity.
worlds.summary: Over the nine-month trial the strips behind the filmed windows lost 12 percent of their original color intensity, while the strips behind the untreated windows lost 45 percent.
worlds.explanationIfShown: Comparing the two conditions means reporting both measured losses, and this summary pairs the notes' 12 percent behind the filmed windows with the 45 percent behind the untreated bank. The other summaries report losses these notes never record — 26 against 31 percent, 19 against 58 percent, and 34 against 49 percent — so each misstates both halves of the comparison.

goal: explain why the finding surprised researchers

notes: - Materials engineer Priya Raghunathan monitored two stadium fields through one playing season: one filled with recycled crumb rubber from scrap tires, the other with virgin sand and cork.
- Probes buried just beneath the turf logged surface temperature every ten minutes.
- Before installation the team predicted the crumb-rubber field would run about 9 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than the sand-and-cork field.
- Across the season the crumb-rubber field instead averaged 2.6 degrees Fahrenheit cooler than the sand-and-cork field.
- The cooler readings appeared only during the morning hours; at other times the two fields stayed within a tenth of a degree of each other.
worlds.summary: Raghunathan's team had predicted that the crumb-rubber field would run about 9 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than the sand-and-cork field, so it was startling that the recycled infill instead averaged 2.6 degrees Fahrenheit cooler, and cooler only during the morning hours.
worlds.explanationIfShown: The surprise these notes describe is a reversal of a specific expectation: a predicted 9 degrees Fahrenheit hotter turned into 2.6 degrees cooler, and only in the morning hours. The other summaries build the surprise from a prediction of 15, 6, or 12 degrees and margins of 1.5, 4.8, or 3.4 degrees confined to the midday, late-afternoon, or evening hours — figures and windows these measurements do not contain.

goal: acknowledge a limitation of the study

notes: - Ingrid Halvorsen installed digital wait-time signs at the Kaldbak ferry terminal's boarding queue.
- The trial ran for three weeks.
- Signs were installed only at the gates serving the late-evening return sailings.
- Reported crowding complaints fell by 22 percent while the signs were in place.
- Halvorsen did not measure whether the signs changed how long passengers actually waited.
worlds.summary: Halvorsen's signs coincided with a 22 percent drop in crowding complaints, but the trial lasted only three weeks and covered only the gates serving the late-evening return sailings, so the effect may not hold across the terminal's other sailings.
worlds.explanationIfShown: These notes record a trial that "ran for three weeks" at "the gates serving the late-evening return sailings," and only this summary names both while framing them as bounds on what the 22 percent drop can show. The other summaries state that the trial lasted "six weeks," "nine weeks," or "twelve weeks" and place the signs at the early-morning commuter, weekend excursion, or midday tourist gates — durations and locations these notes contradict.

goal: emphasize the practical application of the research

notes: - Tomás Ferreira tested a linseed-based wood treatment on public park benches in Aveiro.
- After two years outdoors, treated benches showed 40 percent less surface cracking than untreated benches.
- Per bench, the treatment costs less than the polyurethane varnish the city now applies.
- The advantage was largest for benches in areas with hard winter frosts.
- Crews can reapply the treatment with a brush during ordinary maintenance rounds.
worlds.summary: Ferreira's trial gives park crews something they can act on: a brush-applied linseed treatment that costs less than their current varnish, leaves benches with 40 percent less surface cracking after two years, and pays off most on benches in areas with hard winter frosts.
worlds.explanationIfShown: Only this summary matches these notes on all three facts a maintenance department would act on: the treatment "costs less than the polyurethane varnish the city now applies," it yielded "40 percent less surface cracking," and the advantage was "largest for benches in areas with hard winter frosts." The other summaries price the coating at "about the same as," "slightly more than," or "roughly twice as much as" the current varnish, promise 85, 55, or 70 percent less cracking, and send crews to seafront, woodland-shade, or full-sun benches instead.
